Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.

summaries.gardner: ConocoPhillips has the momentum Gardner likes (up about 67% in the 52 weeks to October 16, 2026) and capable, disciplined management, but it is the largest US independent oil and gas producer in a mature commodity industry, not the top dog in an emerging one. It lacks a hard-to-copy, brand-led advantage, so it fits few Rule Breaker traits.
summaries.buffett: The business is simple to understand and has long-life, low-cost assets (Permian, Alaska, Qatar and Australia LNG), but its earnings swing with oil and gas prices: losses in 2016, 2017 and 2020 and profits from $7,988M (2025) to $18,680M (2022). Returns on capital of about 11-12% are adequate rather than exceptional, and at about 19.5 times trailing earnings there is no clear margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger would respect its capital discipline and its framework of returning a large share of cash flow (targeting 45% of cash from operations in 2026), but it sells a commodity at prices it cannot set. Inverting, an oil-price collapse, cost overruns on long projects like Willow and the energy transition are real ways to lose value, though low debt makes outright failure unlikely.
summaries.lynch: ConocoPhillips is a classic Lynch cyclical, and he warned that cyclicals look cheapest near peak earnings: its forward P/E of about 12.6 rests on 2026 oil prices lifted by the Middle East conflict. The share count is shrinking (diluted shares down about 3.6% in a year), but insiders have been net sellers, not buyers.
summaries.fisher: ConocoPhillips scores on Fisher's points for cost control, long-range planning (Willow first oil expected 2029, LNG growth) and a clear capital framework, but it sells undifferentiated oil and gas with no special selling edge or research-driven new products. Its growth depends more on commodity prices and acquisitions than on innovation.
summaries.graham: It passes Graham's tests for size and financial strength (current ratio 1.54) and has paid dividends every year since its 2002 formation, though it cut the quarterly dividend from $0.74 to $0.25 in 2016. It fails on earnings stability (losses in 2016, 2017 and 2020) and on price: about 19 times three-year average earnings and P/E times P/B of about 52.
summaries.thiel: ConocoPhillips does not fit Thiel's monopoly view: it competes with many producers and national oil companies in a commodity market with no proprietary 10x technology. Its scarce Alaska and LNG assets are valuable but are not a technology-driven monopoly.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner favours secular growth compounders with clear catalysts; ConocoPhillips' 2026 gains came mainly from an oil-price spike, and its revenue of $61,548M in 2025 was well below 2022's $82,156M. It could suit a tactical energy view, but not his long-duration growth style.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller trades macro themes and momentum, and COP has both in 2026: Middle East supply disruption lifted its realized price to $62.33/BOE in Q2 2026 (from $45.77) and the shares rose about 67% in a year. The thesis depends on oil prices staying high, so it fits as a macro trade rather than a long-term concentrated holding.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith avoids cyclical, capital-heavy businesses without pricing power, and ConocoPhillips spends about $12B a year on capital to replace depleting reserves and earns returns on capital of about 11-12%. It would not meet his definition of a good company.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula, ConocoPhillips looks better than the oil majors: EV/EBIT of about 12.9 gives an operating earnings yield near 7.8%, and return on capital is about 11.6%. Those figures are middling rather than top-ranked, and they rest on elevated 2026 commodity prices.
summaries.akre: Akre's stool needs a great business, great management and great reinvestment; ConocoPhillips has disciplined management and reinvests in Willow, LNG and the Permian, but the business is a commodity producer earning modest returns on that capital. It fits one leg at best, and the CEO changed on September 1, 2026.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai buys simple businesses during temporary distress at deep discounts; ConocoPhillips was such a case in 2020, but in October 2026 it trades near 52-week highs after the oil spike. Low debt and low-cost assets limit permanent-loss risk, but the price is not a bargain.
summaries.wood: ConocoPhillips is the opposite of ARK's disruptive-innovation themes; ARK expects electric vehicles and cheaper batteries to reduce oil demand over time. It has no meaningful exposure to AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or genomics.
summaries.ackman: Ackman wants simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with pricing power and low exposure to outside forces; ConocoPhillips generates strong free cash flow (about $10.1B over the last twelve months) but has no pricing power and its earnings depend on commodity prices. It does not fit his core criteria.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's scale-economics-shared model does not apply to a commodity producer selling at market prices. ConocoPhillips' scale lowers its costs, but the benefit is kept as margin and returned to shareholders rather than passed to customers to build loyalty.
summaries.valentine: Valentine looked for huge, fast-growing markets and products solving painful problems at early-stage companies; ConocoPhillips supplies essential energy but in a mature, slow-growing market as a 24-year-old public company. It is far from the kind of opportunity Sequoia backs.
summaries.nash: ConocoPhillips fails Tom Nash's process early: it is a commodity producer, one of his zones to avoid, and debt ($23,290M) exceeds cash and short-term investments ($7,692M), though its trailing operating margin of about 23.6% clears his 20% floor. Revenue fell in 2023 and 2024, trailing growth is about 8.5% and its 13-category score is about 55 of 130. The price implies about 13.5% annual revenue growth and his DCF gives roughly $45 a share against $146.51, so it fails his valuation steps too.

momentum.evidence: COP rose about 67% in the 52 weeks to October 16, 2026 (to $146.51, StockAnalysis), far ahead of the S&P 500's roughly 20% one-year total return, and set a new 52-week high in mid-October.

g4.evidence: Management is respected for its capital discipline under Ryan Lance and now Andy O'Brien (CEO since September 1, 2026), but the stock is held mainly by index and institutional funds (about 86%) rather than famous concentrated investors.

g6.evidence: Some commentators call it fully valued after the 2026 rally (GuruFocus puts its GF Value at $127.32, about 15% below the price), but a forward P/E of about 12.6 is not widely seen as extreme.

simple.evidence: ConocoPhillips finds, produces and sells oil, natural gas and LNG, a business a careful generalist can follow.

b2.evidence: Results swing with commodity prices: net losses in 2016 (-$3,615M), 2017 (-$855M) and 2020 (-$2,701M), and net income of $18,680M in 2022 versus $7,988M in 2025.

integrity.evidence: Management has kept a clear, published capital framework (returning 45% of cash from operations targeted in 2026) and reports candidly, but insiders sold about $145.9M of stock in the past year while buying only about $0.5M (GuruFocus).

b6.evidence: Deals like Concho (2021) and Marathon Oil ($22.5B, closed November 2024) fit its low cost-of-supply strategy, but they were also part of an industry-wide consolidation race.

roic.evidence: ROIC is about 11.6% (StockAnalysis) with modest debt ($23,290M against $65,349M of equity at June 30, 2026), decent but not high and not consistent across the cycle (losses in 2020).

fcf.evidence: Over the last twelve months to June 30, 2026, operating cash flow of $21,925M less capital spending of $11,861M left free cash flow of $10,064M, above net income of $9,282M.

b10.evidence: Retained earnings rose to $72,921M and funded Permian, Alaska and LNG growth, but the shares fell sharply in 2015-2016 and 2020, so retained profits did not always add matching market value.

safety.evidence: At $146.51, about 19.5 times trailing earnings and above GuruFocus's GF Value of $127.32, the price offers no margin of safety against a fall in oil prices.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E of about 12.6 looks reasonable, but it rests on 2026 oil prices that may ease, and consensus 2027 revenue ($67.24B) is below 2026 ($71.0B).

mu5.evidence: Low debt and low-cost assets make bankruptcy unlikely, but oil-price collapses, project overruns (Willow), geopolitics and the energy transition are several plausible ways to lose value.

reinvest.evidence: It can reinvest in Willow (first oil expected 2029), LNG and the Permian at decent returns, but returns depend on oil prices and reserves deplete.

ly2.evidence: It is a classic cyclical whose story is low-cost Permian and LNG volumes plus a targeted $7B free-cash-flow inflection by 2029.

ly3.evidence: A trailing P/E of about 19.5 is well above its long-run earnings growth; diluted EPS fell from $14.57 in 2022 to $6.35 in 2025 before the 2026 rebound.

runway.evidence: Total revenues and other income were $61,548M in 2025, below $82,156M in 2022, and long-term oil demand growth is slow.

ly7.evidence: Diluted shares fell from 1,258,998K in Q2 2025 to 1,214,255K in Q2 2026 (about 3.6%) through buybacks, but insiders were net sellers of about $145.4M over the past year.

ly8.evidence: COP is a large, widely followed S&P 500 stock covered by about 28 analysts.

fi2.evidence: It is developing new supply such as Willow, Port Arthur LNG and 12 MTPA of LNG offtake, but these are more oil and gas, not new products.

fi3.evidence: It spends little on formal R&D, though its Optimized Cascade LNG process and longer-lateral shale drilling show practical technical results.

fi4.evidence: It sells commodities at market prices through its marketing arm; there is no evidence of an unusual selling edge.

longterm.evidence: It invests in long-cycle projects like Willow and LNG, but its framework also commits a large share of cash flow to near-term buybacks and dividends ($5.0B of repurchases in 2025).

gr1.evidence: It is the largest US independent oil and gas producer, with a market value of about $176B and production of 2,248 MBOED in Q2 2026.

ni10.evidence: It reported net losses in 2016 (-$3,615M), 2017 (-$855M) and 2020 (-$2,701M).

gr4.evidence: It has paid a dividend every year since its formation in the August 2002 Conoco-Phillips merger, though it cut the quarterly dividend from $0.74 to $0.25 in February 2016.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS went from -$3.58 in 2015 to $6.35 in 2025 (three-year average from -$2.40 to $7.74), but measured from 2014's $5.51 the gain is only about 15%.

gr6.evidence: The price of $146.51 is about 19 times average 2023-2025 diluted EPS of $7.74.

gr7.evidence: A trailing P/E of about 19.5 times a P/B of about 2.69 gives about 52, well above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Its oil and gas are commodities; it has no proprietary technology ten times better than rivals.

timing.evidence: The 2026 Middle East supply disruption lifted its realized price to $62.33/BOE in Q2 2026, but long-term oil demand faces the energy transition.

th3.evidence: It did not start by dominating a small market; it was formed in 2002 by merging two large oil companies.

team.evidence: Ryan Lance built a respected returns-focused strategy over 14 years, and successor Andy O'Brien (CEO since September 1, 2026) is a long-time insider and former CFO, but neither is an exceptional founder.
